5010: Lieutenant (Лейтенант) — In the wartime and early postwar Soviet Air Force, lieutenant was the normal entry rank for a fully commissioned pilot and is therefore a suitable starting rank for a Korean War career. Its shoulder boards carried two small stars, reflecting the Soviet system introduced with the restoration of traditional shoulder boards in 1943; junior officers used small stars and a single longitudinal “clearance” stripe. A lieutenant would normally serve as a line pilot while gaining operational experience before being entrusted with formation leadership. Soviet pilots sent to Korea retained their actual Soviet ranks even though they operated covertly under the 64th Fighter Aviation Corps and generally appeared publicly in Chinese or North Korean guise.
5011: Senior Lieutenant (Старший лейтенант) — The next junior-officer grade, marked by three small stars on the same single-stripe officer shoulder board. The rank indicated an officer who had moved beyond the newly commissioned stage and could be trusted with greater tactical responsibility, often including leading a pair or flight element. Many Soviet fighter pilots in Korea were already experienced World War II veterans, so the rank did not necessarily imply limited combat experience. Its three-star arrangement formed a clear visual step between lieutenant and captain without changing the basic junior-officer shoulder-board pattern.
5012: Captain (Капитан) — A senior company-grade officer rank distinguished by four small stars, still worn on the single-stripe junior-officer board. In Soviet aviation, a captain was commonly an experienced pilot and was a very plausible rank for a zveno (звено) commander, leading a small tactical formation of aircraft. The four-star arrangement represented the highest grade in the junior-officer series before the insignia changed markedly at major. In Korea, a captain could therefore be both an active fighter pilot and a formation leader rather than simply a staff officer.
5013: Major (Майор) — The first Soviet field-grade rank, identified by one larger star and shoulder boards with two longitudinal clearance stripes instead of the single stripe used by captains and lieutenants. The change in both star size and board design deliberately made the transition to senior officer status immediately visible. In an aviation regiment, majors frequently served as squadron commanders, operations officers, or other senior flying leaders. A Soviet eskadrilya (эскадрилья) commander in Korea would therefore very plausibly have held the rank of major.
5014: Lieutenant Colonel (Подполковник) — A senior field-grade rank represented by two large stars on the two-stripe officer shoulder board. Lieutenant colonels commonly served as deputy regimental commanders, chiefs of staff, squadron commanders in important units, or occasionally as regimental commanders themselves. The two large stars continued the field-grade progression begun with the major while preserving the same basic shoulder-board construction. Within the highly experienced Soviet formations deployed to Korea, officers of this rank often combined extensive World War II combat experience with responsibility for supervising younger pilots and coordinating regiment-level operations.
5015: Colonel (Полковник) — The highest normal field-grade rank, marked by three large stars on a two-stripe shoulder board. Colonels were typical commanders of aviation regiments, including fighter aviation regiments (IAP — истребительный авиационный полк), and were responsible for the combat effectiveness of several squadrons rather than a single formation. The three-star insignia visually completed the Soviet senior-officer sequence of major, lieutenant colonel, and colonel. In Korea, a colonel commanding an IAP would oversee tactics, readiness, pilot assignments, and combat operations while still belonging to a force whose Soviet identity was officially concealed.
5016: Major General (Генерал-майор) — The first Soviet general-officer rank and, despite the name “major general,” the equivalent of a one-star general in Western rank comparisons. Its shoulder board carried one large general’s star and abandoned the longitudinal clearance stripes used by colonels, replacing them with the distinctive general-officer board and its more elaborate gold pattern. Major generals commonly commanded aviation divisions or held senior corps and air-army staff positions. The visual break from the colonel’s shoulder board emphasized that promotion to general was not simply another step in the field-grade sequence but entry into an entirely different command level.
5017: Lieutenant General (Генерал-лейтенант) — A two-star general in the Soviet system, with two large stars mounted on the distinctive stripe-less general-officer shoulder board. Officers of this rank could command aviation corps or occupy senior air-army and theater-level positions, directing several divisions and thousands of personnel rather than individual squadrons or regiments. The 64th Fighter Aviation Corps (64-й ИАК) that controlled Soviet fighter operations in Korea was commanded at this level during important periods of the war, making lieutenant general an especially appropriate top rank for a Soviet Korean War career. Unlike the pilots beneath them, such commanders were concerned primarily with the strategic employment of the Soviet air contingent, coordination with Chinese and North Korean forces, and maintaining the secrecy surrounding direct Soviet participation.
5020: Zhōngwèi (中尉) — In the game, this is the entry officer rank and corresponds approximately to lieutenant. Under the 1955 PLA rank system, a Zhōngwèi wore two small stars on a shoulder board with one longitudinal stripe, following the Soviet-influenced structure adopted during the PLA’s postwar professionalization. Historically, however, the PLA had no formal military rank system during the Korean War; officers were identified primarily by appointments and cadre grades, so the game applies the 1955 title retroactively.
5021: Shàngwèi (上尉) — Roughly equivalent to captain, this was the next step in the junior-officer sequence and was represented in the 1955 system by three small stars on a single-stripe shoulder board. The insignia followed the same visual progression as contemporary Soviet junior-officer ranks, while the PLAAF distinguished itself through its own Air Force branch colors. For a Korean War setting, the title is necessarily retrospective: Chinese pilots fighting in 1950–1953 did not yet possess formal ranks such as Shàngwèi, even though officers performed comparable flight- and squadron-level duties.
5022: Dàwèi (大尉) — Usually translated as Senior Captain, Dàwèi was an additional company-grade rank placed above captain and below major, closely reflecting the Soviet-style rank structure adopted by the PLA in 1955. Its insignia consisted of four small stars on the same single-stripe shoulder board, completing the junior-officer series. There is no close modern U.S. Air Force equivalent, which makes it a useful intermediate progression rank in the game. Dàwèi did not exist formally during the Korean War itself and is therefore applied retroactively to represent an experienced junior officer of roughly comparable standing.
5023: Shàoxiào (少校) — Equivalent to major, Shàoxiào marked the transition into the PLA’s field-grade officer ranks. The 1955 insignia changed noticeably from the junior-officer pattern: one star was worn with two longitudinal stripes, making promotion from Dàwèi immediately recognizable. An officer at this level would plausibly hold substantial squadron or regiment staff responsibilities, although wartime Chinese appointments were determined by position and cadre grade rather than rank. Thus, for Korea, Shàoxiào is a 1955 designation applied retrospectively to officers who had occupied comparable levels of responsibility in 1950–1953.
5024: Zhōngxiào (中校) — Approximately equivalent to lieutenant colonel, this rank was represented by two stars on a two-stripe field-grade shoulder board. The combination of increasing star count and two longitudinal stripes closely paralleled Soviet rank-insignia logic and reflected the strong Soviet influence on the PLA’s first formal rank system. Officers of comparable standing could serve in senior squadron, regiment, or staff positions. During the Korean War, however, such men did not formally hold the rank Zhōngxiào; the game uses the later 1955 title as a convenient historical progression.
5025: Shàngxiào (上校) — Corresponding broadly to colonel, Shàngxiào carried three stars on the two-stripe field-grade shoulder board introduced with the 1955 rank system. This was a senior command rank appropriate to officers entrusted with major unit or headquarters responsibilities, including positions around regimental level. The insignia deliberately continued the one-, two-, three-star progression used for major through colonel, making the hierarchy readily visible. In a Korean War career it remains an anachronistic label by design, because the PLA did not formally introduce Shàngxiào or any other military rank until 1955.
5026: Dàxiào (大校) — Usually translated as Senior Colonel, Dàxiào occupied the unusual position between colonel and major general and has no exact Western equivalent. Its 1955 insignia used four stars on a two-stripe field-grade shoulder board, extending the field-officer sequence one step beyond Shàngxiào. The rank was characteristic of the Soviet-influenced “Eastern” system adopted by the PLA and provided an additional grade for senior commanders who had not yet entered the general-officer corps. As with all of these PRC ranks, Dàxiào did not formally exist during the Korean War and is being used retrospectively in the game for officers of comparable seniority.
5027: Shàojiàng (少将) — Major General and the first general-officer grade in the 1955 PLA system, represented by one general’s star on a gold general-officer shoulder board rather than the two-striped boards of the field grades. This visual break emphasized the transition from senior regimental-level leadership into command and staff responsibilities at division level and above. The broader 1955 system was heavily influenced by Soviet practice, although Chinese service colors and insignia details gave the PLAAF its own identity. No Chinese officer fighting in Korea formally held the rank Shàojiàng at the time; the game applies the title retroactively to represent officers who occupied comparable high-level command positions before formal ranks were introduced in October 1955.
5030: Chungwi (중위) — Roughly equivalent to lieutenant, Chungwi was a junior commissioned-officer rank in the Korean People’s Army and Air Force during the Korean War. The KPA’s rank system, introduced with the new armed forces in the late 1940s, was strongly influenced by Soviet practice, and its officer insignia consequently followed a similar hierarchy of stars and shoulder-board distinctions. A Chungwi in the air force would typically be a relatively junior pilot or officer still building operational experience. This was therefore a natural early-career rank for a North Korean fighter pilot flying Soviet-supplied aircraft such as the Yak-9 or, later, MiG types.
5031: Sangwi (상위) — Usually translated as Senior Lieutenant, Sangwi represented an experienced junior officer above Chungwi but below captain. The title and its place in the hierarchy reflected the Soviet-style progression that strongly influenced the early KPA, including the use of an additional lieutenant grade not normally found in the U.S. system. In the air force, an officer of this grade could already be an experienced combat pilot and take responsibility for leading small formations. During the Korean War, practical flying experience often mattered at least as much as nominal rank because the young North Korean air arm had entered the conflict with relatively few fully combat-qualified pilots.
5032: Taewi (대위) — Corresponding broadly to captain, Taewi was the senior junior-officer grade in the Korean People’s Army’s Soviet-influenced rank structure. In an aviation unit, a captain could serve as an experienced formation leader, instructor, staff officer, or commander of a small flying element. The rank sat immediately below the transition into field-grade officer status and therefore represented an important step from individual pilot toward unit leadership. For a Korean War career, Taewi is particularly appropriate for a combat-experienced pilot beginning to assume regular command responsibilities.
5033: Sojwa (소좌) — Equivalent to major, Sojwa marked the beginning of the field-grade officer ranks. As in the Soviet system that inspired it, promotion to major represented more than simply another junior-officer step: the officer was increasingly expected to manage larger formations, operations, and staff responsibilities. Within the Korean People’s Air Force, a Sojwa could plausibly serve in squadron-level leadership or an important operational staff position. The Soviet influence was especially strong in the North Korean air arm, whose organization, training, aircraft, and early doctrine were heavily shaped by Soviet assistance.
5034: Chungjwa (중좌) — Approximately equivalent to lieutenant colonel, Chungjwa was a senior field-grade rank associated with substantial command or staff responsibility. The rank formed part of the Soviet-derived progression from major through lieutenant colonel and colonel, a structure adopted by the newly established North Korean armed forces. In an aviation context, an officer of this level might serve as a deputy unit commander, senior operations officer, or commander of a significant flying formation. By the Korean War, such officers were operating within an air force that had developed rapidly from the Soviet-style aviation organizations created in North Korea after 1945.
5035: Sangjwa (상좌) — Broadly equivalent to colonel, Sangjwa was a high field-grade rank suitable for commanders of major aviation units or senior headquarters officers. Its place in the hierarchy closely followed the Soviet model, reflecting the considerable organizational and doctrinal influence Moscow had on the early KPA. A Sangjwa in the air force would normally be concerned with the operations and readiness of an entire unit rather than simply leading individual combat formations. During the Korean War, officers at this level were responsible for rebuilding and directing North Korean air operations after the heavy losses suffered during the opening months of the conflict.
5036: Taejwa (대좌) — Usually rendered as Senior Colonel, Taejwa occupied the distinctive grade between colonel and general officer and has no exact U.S. Air Force equivalent. This additional senior-officer step was characteristic of Soviet-influenced military hierarchies and allowed experienced commanders to advance beyond colonel without immediately entering the general ranks. In the Korean People’s Army, it could be associated with very senior regimental, divisional, or headquarters responsibilities. For the game, Taejwa provides a useful final field-grade step before promotion into the general-officer command structure.
5037: Sojang (소장) — Major General and the first general-officer rank, Sojang represented entry into the highest levels of Korean People’s Army command. Like the Soviet General-Major, which strongly influenced the North Korean system, it corresponds functionally to a one-star general despite the English title “Major General.” Officers at this level could command major formations or occupy senior air-force and headquarters positions rather than participate routinely as line pilots. The rank therefore marks the transition from tactical aviation leadership to responsibility for the planning, organization, and employment of large elements of the North Korean air arm.
6010: Second Lieutenant (2nd Lt.) — The entry-level commissioned officer rank in the U.S. Air Force, typically held by newly commissioned pilots and other junior officers during the Korean War. Its insignia was a single gold bar, inherited directly from the U.S. Army officer rank system when the Air Force became an independent service in 1947. The gold bar distinguished a second lieutenant from the silver bar of a first lieutenant, and the Army-style grade insignia remained in use even as the new Air Force developed its own blue uniforms and service identity. In Korea, many second lieutenants were young pilots arriving from advanced flight training and gaining their first combat experience in fighters, bombers, transports, or reconnaissance units.
6011: First Lieutenant (1st Lt.) — A junior commissioned officer rank, normally reached after a second lieutenant had gained some experience in operational service. Its insignia was a single silver bar, continuing the U.S. Army rank system inherited by the Air Force when it became an independent service in 1947. The somewhat counterintuitive use of silver for the higher grade and gold for second lieutenant came from long-established Army insignia traditions in which silver devices often denoted the senior version of a paired rank. During the Korean War, first lieutenants were common among operational pilots and could already be experienced combat aviators with substantial numbers of missions.
6012: Captain (Capt.) — A company-grade officer rank represented by two parallel silver bars, traditionally nicknamed “railroad tracks.” The insignia evolved naturally from the single bar of a first lieutenant and had been used by Army officers long before the creation of the independent Air Force. In Korean War flying units, captains frequently served as experienced pilots, flight leaders, instructors, or staff officers, and some commanded small operational elements. For many combat aviators, captain was the rank at which considerable flying experience and increasing leadership responsibility came together.
6013: Major (Maj.) — The first field-grade officer rank, identified by a gold oak leaf. The oak leaf originated in 19th-century U.S. military insignia and became the established symbol for majors and lieutenant colonels, with gold denoting the junior of the two grades. During the Korean War, Air Force majors commonly held positions such as flight or squadron operations officers, experienced combat leaders, and headquarters staff officers. A major might therefore combine extensive flying experience with responsibility for planning and directing the missions of other aircrews.
6014: Lieutenant Colonel (Lt. Col.) — A senior field-grade rank distinguished by a silver oak leaf, the silver version indicating a grade above the major’s gold leaf. This gold-to-silver progression was inherited directly from U.S. Army tradition and remained unchanged when the Air Force became independent. During the Korean War, lieutenant colonels frequently commanded squadrons or held important operations and staff positions within groups and wings. Many were highly experienced officers whose careers had begun before or during World War II and who brought that combat experience into the jet age.
6015: Colonel (Col.) — The highest field-grade rank, represented by a silver spread-winged eagle, one of the most recognizable American officer insignia. The eagle had been associated with the rank of colonel in the U.S. Army since the 19th century and was retained unchanged by the new Air Force after 1947. During the Korean War, colonels commonly commanded groups or wings and occupied senior operational and headquarters positions. Officers of this grade often bridged two very different eras of military aviation, having begun their careers with piston-engined aircraft before overseeing operations involving aircraft such as the F-86 Sabre and other early jets.
6016: Brigadier General (Brig. Gen.) — The first general-officer rank, identified by one silver five-pointed star. Stars had been used to identify American general officers since the 19th century, with the number of stars providing an immediately recognizable indication of grade. During the Korean War, brigadier generals could command major Air Force organizations or serve in senior staff and deputy-command positions responsible for coordinating large-scale air operations. The single-star insignia marked the officer’s transition from field-grade command into the general-officer leadership structure.
6017: Major General (Maj. Gen.) — A senior general-officer rank represented by two silver stars, normally worn side by side on the uniform. The two-star system continued the traditional American practice of distinguishing general-officer grades simply by increasing the number of stars, making rank readily identifiable at a glance. During the Korean War, major generals commanded major formations such as air divisions or held senior positions in numbered air forces and theater-level headquarters. At this level, an officer was generally concerned less with individual missions and more with directing air campaigns, allocating forces, and coordinating fighter, bomber, reconnaissance, transport, and support operations across a large theater.
